rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Ka = acoustic root of the abhiipśātmaka āśā vṛtti (the propensity of hope), which goads creatures — especially humans — to work in various ways. Etymology: ka (kae + ḍa) = 'that which produces sound'; also 'water' (flowing water; va = water in general); also 'hair grown on the head' (kac = glossy). Ka + iisha = kesha (hair; also Nārāyaṇa). Kārya Brahma (Saguṇarasātmaka Brahma), represented by ka, is the controller of the living world; Buddhist Saṃvṛtti Bodhicitta = the created world = Kārya Brahma (kāpālika: 'Kaṃ saṃvṛtti bodhicittaṃ pālayati').

These are cosmological / etymological ASSOCIATIONS of ka, NOT poles.

rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: The acoustic root of āśā vṛtti is ka; that of cintā vṛtti (the propensity of worry) is kha. If your train runs late you think not only of the delay but of the probable inconveniences (the host, arriving late for food, deciding to eat near the station) — such consequential thoughts are symbolized by kha. Travelling elsewhere you might reflect on a collapsing brassware industry and whether it could be revived, though you are 'not personally affected' and 'not a direct player in your own thoughts' — such impersonal thoughts are also kha. Kha MEANS 'sky' but is NOT the acoustic root of the sky (that is ha); kha also means 'heaven', but only its CRUDE aspects — the sphere of heaven that transcends the crude is kṣa. Ka = Kārya Brahma is the first consonant; and since ka + ha = kha, kha immediately follows ka in the Indo-Aryan alphabet.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: Paired with ka: ka = āśā (hope) goads action; kha = cintā (worry / objective thought) reflects. kha MEANS 'sky' and 'heaven' but is NOT their acoustic root — the SKY's root is ha; kha = the CRUDE aspects of heaven, while the transcendent sphere = kṣa (ksha). Structurally ka + ha = kha (hence kha follows ka, the first consonant / Kārya Brahma, in the alphabet). These are meanings/associations, NOT poles.

attested_associations.value: MEANS 'sky'/'heaven' (crude aspects) but is NOT their acoustic root (ha is)
transcendent heaven = kṣa (ksha)

rows.sanskrit_label: Ceṣṭā (effort / striving to arouse dormant potential)
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Every entity has the potentiality of expression; an animate entity can arouse that dormant potentiality through both internal and external means. If poetic genius lies dormant in someone and he arouses it by applying his will-force, he becomes a renowned poet; if lethargy prevents it, the genius stays unexpressed. The effort made to arouse one's dormant potentiality is called ceṣṭā. Ceṣṭā is one of the psychic vṛttis and is the MAIN CAUSE of mundane development AND spiritual elevation — its value in the mundane and supramundane spheres is immense. Ga, the acoustic root of ceṣṭā, plays an important role in the physical, psychic and spiritual spheres.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: ceṣṭā = the effort to arouse dormant potentiality (latent genius -> applied will-force -> expression; else unexpressed). Described as the MAIN CAUSE of BOTH mundane development AND spiritual elevation, operating across the physical, psychic and spiritual spheres. (Scope/significance of the vṛtti — NOT a separate cosmological association.)

attested_associations.value: ceṣṭā = main cause of BOTH mundane development AND spiritual elevation (physical/psychic/spiritual)

rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Mamatā, the vṛtti of love and attachment, is related to time, space and individuality. People praise even the poorest goods made in their own country and criticize the best goods made elsewhere — irrational attachment for a place, a psychic disease (SPACE). A mother who sacrifices everything for her child mercilessly slices living kai fish without feeling, deaf to their agony (INDIVIDUALITY). The mother cow who lovingly licks her calf today kicks it away when it grows tomorrow (TIME). Thus mamatā is limited by the relative factors. Only human beings can make mamatā TRANSCEND the boundaries of time, space and individuality, after persistent and intense effort — impossible for other beings. Gha is the acoustic root of mamatā vṛtti.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: mamatā is related to time, space and individuality; its bounded form shows as place-attachment (praising one's own poor goods over better foreign ones — a 'psychic disease'), individuality (the mother who cherishes her child yet slices kai fish unmoved), and time (the cow that licks its calf today, kicks it away grown tomorrow). (Illustrations/scope of the vṛtti — not a separate cosmological association.)

attested_associations.value: mamatā bounded by time, space, individuality (illustrations only)

rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Uṋa (ṅa) is the acoustic root of dambha vṛtti (vanity). The popular story: the sage Vashiṣṭha travelled to China to learn the Chinese school of Tantra, learned the use of una in Tantric mantras, and introduced it in India; una is used extensively across the Indo-Chinese languages (Tibetan, Ladakhi, Sherpa, Manpa). Its transmission is linked to the Tárā cult, trifurcated as Ugra/Vajra Tárā (India), Nīla Tárā / Nīla Sarasvatī (Tibet), and Bhrāmarī / Kṛṣṇa Tárā (China). The acoustic root of Vajra Tárā and Nīla Tárā is aeṃ; that of the black Bhrāmarī Tárā (= Kālī in Varṇāśrama Dharma) is krīṃ (ka = Kārya Brahma + ra = the luminous factor).
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: Phonetic-historical (NOT poles): per the legend, una was learned by Vashiṣṭha in China and introduced to India, and is used across the Indo-Chinese languages (Tibetan/Ladakhi/Sherpa/Manpa). Its transmission is tied to the Tárā cult — but the Tárā deities have their OWN acoustic roots (aeṃ for Vajra/Nīla Tárā; krīṃ = ka[Kārya Brahma] + ra[luminous factor] for Bhrāmarī Tárā / Kālī), NOT una. Record as history/association; do not fold aeṃ/krīṃ/Tárā into nga's poles.

attested_associations.value: legend: uṋa learned by Vashiṣṭha in China; used across Indo-Chinese languages (Tibetan/Ladakhi/Sherpa/Manpa)
Tárā cult transmission — but Tárā roots are aeṃ / krīṃ, NOT ṅa

Example (Howrah station): asked whether the Uluberia local has left, one gentleman snaps abusively ('Am I a railway timetable?... People like you make life hell...') — uncontrolled vitarka; a second replies helpfully with just the relevant facts (platform eleven, five minutes) — pramita vāk (balanced statement, only relevant words).

rows.sanskrit_label: Piśunatā (senseless / sadistic cruelty — torturous killing, malice)
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Senseless, sadistic killing is called piśunatā vṛtti. Slaughtering in the way that inflicts the LEAST pain is NOT piśunatā; but killing slowly and cruelly — first chopping off legs, then tail, then head — is definitely piśunatā. (A live tortoise part-chopped and left crawling in its own blood; criminals impaled on spikes, half-buried and salted for dogs, or flayed alive — all examples of piśunatā.) The killing of animals, however done, is contrary to the spirit of Neohumanism.

rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Ta is the acoustic root of staticity, long sleep and deep sleep; also of intellectual dullness and spiritual inertness. That which brings about the cessation of dullness and staticity is Tantra — 'Taṃ jāḍyāt tārayet yastu sa tantraḥ'. The root-verb tan means 'to expand'; if a rope-bound person expands his body the ropes snap of themselves — that which liberates through tan (expansion) is also Tantra — 'Taṃ vistāreṇa tārayet yastu sah tantraḥ'.

rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Na is the acoustic root of moha vṛtti (blind attachment / infatuation), usually divided into four categories — time, space, idea, individuality. deshagata moha ('geo-sentiment') = losing rationality out of blind attachment for one's country (praising a barren, starving, food-importing land as abundant). kālagata moha = blind attachment to a period of time (old-timers who 'could digest iron pans' disparaging the present age). idea = a strong idea pulls the mind back again and again (the thief who broods on the crime scene and returns into the police's hands). ādhāragata moha = fascination for a long-used object (a rich man's attachment to a battered one-armed chair; a bell-metal pot that broke up a family). The only way to free oneself is to superimpose the ideation of INDIFFERENCE and divert one's thoughts toward Parama Puruṣa; intimidation or laws control it only temporarily — the mind is sublimated by spiritual ideation, not by high-sounding philosophy.

Attested cure / liberating direction: superimpose the ideation of indifference and divert thoughts to Parama Puruṣa — sublimation by spiritual ideation, NOT by law or philosophy. Cross-ref: the moha ripu underlies the pa fetter of hatred/fear.

attested_associations.value: moha divides into four: space/time/idea/individuality; cure = indifference + Parama Puruṣa

rows.sanskrit_label: Avajñā (indifference / neglect of what has value)
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Ba is the acoustic root of avajñā vṛtti (indifference). Ignoring something actually UNACCEPTABLE is upekṣā; NEGLECTING something which may actually have VALUE is avajñā (~ avahelā, a negative term; upekṣā is not always bad). The Yoga-sūtra four attitudes (maitrī-karuṇā-muditā-upekṣā): develop maitrī (benign gladness) toward the happy ('may he stay that way'), karuṇā (compassion) toward the miserable, muditā (goodwill) toward the virtuous ('let his intellect inspire him'), and upekṣā (indifference — 'that's his own business') toward the wicked — BUT if the person's sinful actions harm society, one can no longer afford to be indifferent.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: Distinctions: avajñā (neglect of the valuable) vs upekṣā (ignoring the unacceptable — not always bad) vs avahelā (negative disregard). The brahmavihāra four attitudes: maitrī (happy), karuṇā (suffering), muditā (virtuous), upekṣā (wicked) — with the caveat that indifference to SOCIALLY-HARMFUL wickedness is not acceptable.

attested_associations.value: brahmavihāra four attitudes: maitrī/karuṇā/muditā/upekṣā

rows.classical_associations_verbatim: la = kṣititattva (the solid / earth factor, dharaṇī / pṛthvī); the LAM bīja mantra (four-sided/square, deep-yellow — 'Laṃ bījaṃ dharaṇīṃ dhyāyet'). ('Earth-bound hardness' echoes this solid factor.) An element/bīja association, distinct from the kruratā pole.

attested_associations.value: kṣititattva (solid/earth factor, dharaṇī / pṛthvī)
LAM bīja — four-sided/square, deep-yellow ('Laṃ bījaṃ dharaṇīṃ dhyāyet')

rows.sanskrit_label: Dharma (ensconcement in one's original stance / that which sustains) — with jalatattva (water) association; classical side liberating-oriented
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Va is the acoustic root of dharma — 'ensconcement in one's original stance'. The innate propensity of human beings is to move toward subtlety in the psychic/spiritual spheres and finally merge into Parama Puruṣa; this unbroken movement is mānava dharma. 'Sukhaṃ vāñchati sarvo hi... ' (all beings long for happiness; dharma originates from that innate propensity, so dharma should be observed by all). 'Dhriyate dharma ityāhuḥ' — dharma is that which SUSTAINS. To diverge from dharma is to rush toward total annihilation. Va is ALSO the acoustic root of jalatattva (the liquid factor — water and any liquid) and of the rain-god Varuṇa Deva.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: va = jalatattva (the liquid factor — water and any liquid) and the rain-god Varuṇa Deva. Dharma = 'that which sustains' (dhriyate dharma); the innate longing for happiness is its origin ('sukhaṃ vāñchati sarvo hi'); diverging from dharma rushes toward annihilation. (Element/deity association, distinct from the dharma pole.)

attested_associations.value: jalatattva (liquid factor — water and any liquid)
Varuṇa Deva (the rain-god)
dharma ('that which sustains'; dhriyate dharma) — the four-varga longing assigned to va

rows.sanskrit_label: Kāma (physical / worldly desire) — with tamoguṇa (the static principle) association
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Śa is the acoustic root of tamoguṇa (the static principle), and also of all kinds of worldly desires — wealth, opulence, name, fame, social position. The collective Sanskrit term is kāma. The four recognized longings of human life are dharma (psycho-spiritual), artha (psychic), kāma (PHYSICAL), and mokṣa (spiritual / liberation). kāma = all types of PHYSICAL longings.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: śa = tamoguṇa (the static principle). The four puruṣārthas (longings): dharma (psycho-spiritual), artha (psychic), kāma (physical), mokṣa (liberation) — kāma = all physical longings. (Guṇa association + longing-hierarchy frame.)

attested_associations.value: tamoguṇa (the static principle)
kāma (physical longing) — the four-varga puruṣārtha for śa

rows.sanskrit_label: Mokṣa (unqualified liberation / salvation) — with sattvaguṇa (the sentient principle) association; classical side liberating-oriented
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Sa is the acoustic root of mokṣa (salvation, unqualified liberation) and of sattvaguṇa (the sentient principle). In the four-varga scheme: va = dharma (+ liquid factor); ṣa ('sha') = artha (removal of worldly wants) + rajoguṇa; śa = kāma (worldly/physical wants) + tamoguṇa; sa = mokṣa + sattvaguṇa.
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: sa = sattvaguṇa (the sentient principle) and mokṣa (unqualified liberation) — the highest of the four longings (dharma/artha/kāma/mokṣa). Part of the four-varga sibilant scheme: śa(sha)=tamoguṇa/kāma, ṣa(ssa)=rajoguṇa/artha, sa=sattvaguṇa/mokṣa.

attested_associations.value: sattvaguṇa (the sentient principle)
mokṣa (liberation) — the four-varga puruṣārtha for sa

rows.sanskrit_label: Artha (psychic longing / worldly purpose — removal of worldly wants) — with rajoguṇa (the mutative principle) association
rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar (four-varga passage): ṣa ('sha') is the acoustic root of artha — 'the removal of worldly wants' — and of rajoguṇa (the mutative principle). artha is the PSYCHIC longing among the four (dharma/artha/kāma/mokṣa).
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: ṣa = rajoguṇa (the mutative principle); artha = the psychic longing / the means that removes worldly wants. Part of the four-varga sibilant scheme (śa=tamoguṇa/kāma, ṣa=rajoguṇa/artha, sa=sattva/mokṣa).

attested_associations.value: rajoguṇa (the mutative principle)
artha (psychic longing / removal of worldly wants) — four-varga puruṣārtha for ṣa

rows.source_quote_verbatim: Sarkar: Kṣa is the acoustic root of mundane knowledge, and also of material science. [Complement to ha = parā-vidyā (intuitional / higher knowledge). In the kha passage, kṣa also represents the sphere of heaven that TRANSCENDS the crude, while kha = the crude aspects of heaven.]
rows.classical_associations_verbatim: kṣa = the complement of ha (parā-vidyā, intuitional knowledge): kṣa is aparā-vidyā (mundane / material knowledge). In the kha passage kṣa also = the sphere of heaven that TRANSCENDS the crude (kha = crude heaven). Structurally kṣa = ka (Kārya Brahma) + ṣa. Classical side liberating-oriented.
